summary: This informational document describes how Virtual Private LAN Service should interoperate with customer bridges. VPLS should offer the same service customers know from bridged networks of their own. It discusses what behaviors are needed to achieve this.

eli5.summary: A company wants its offices to feel like one big local network even though a provider carries the traffic. This explains how to make the provider's service play nicely with the company's switches.

how does vpls work with customer bridges

subtitle: How to deliver Ethernet service to customer bridges over VPLS networks.

tldr.problem: Virtual Private LAN Service should deliver the same Ethernet experience to customers with bridges as they get from their own networks, but customer bridges raise special issues around protocol handling, topology, redundancy and multicast.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes how to build VPLS Provider Edges with an 802.1ad-based bridge module that can handle customer VLANs, service VLANs, topology changes, and bridge protocols like Spanning Tree transparently.
tldr.outcome: By properly modeling the PE as a bridge following IEEE 802.1ad standards, most interoperability challenges with customer edge bridges can be solved within the bridge module rather than burdening the VPLS forwarding side.

today: RFC 6246 is an Informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It remains the primary reference for understanding how VPLS can be architectured to properly support customer edge bridges. While newer VPLS variants and all-optical Ethernet services have been developed, the principles outlined here continue to apply when legacy bridges are in use.

sections.title: VPLS and Customer Bridges
sections.content:
Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) is a service that emulates a local area network over a wide-area IP or MPLS network. One of its main uses is connecting customer edge (CE) devices, which can be routers, servers, or IEEE bridges. When CE devices are bridges, the provider edge (PE) must handle several bridging protocols and behaviors that would not be needed for router-only networks.

This RFC documents the issues that arise when customer edge devices are IEEE bridges and proposes solutions based on the IEEE 802.1ad standard for provider bridges. The approach separates the VPLS PE into a bridge module (following 802.1ad) and a LAN emulation module (following IETF standards), so most bridge-specific problems are handled in the bridge layer rather than the VPLS layer.
sections.eli5: When a company's offices have switches, not just routers, a provider must understand how switches work so it can pretend that all the offices are plugged into the same big switch.

sections.title: The PE Model with Bridge Module
sections.content:
The VPLS-capable PE is structured with a bridge module based on the IEEE 802.1ad provider bridge standard. The bridge module contains two sub-components: an S-VLAN (service VLAN) bridge that is always required, and a C-VLAN (customer VLAN) bridge component that is required only when customer attachment circuits are VLANs.

The S-VLAN bridge tags customer traffic with service VLAN identifiers as it enters the PE and strips those tags as it leaves toward the VPLS forwarders. The C-VLAN bridge component, when present, handles service selection based on customer VLAN tags. This two-layer approach mirrors what the customer's network does locally, so bridging protocols can operate naturally across the service.
sections.eli5: The PE has layers like a bridge does: one layer that handles the company's labels (C-VLAN) and one that handles the provider's labels (S-VLAN), so bridging protocols work the same way in both places.

sections.title: Mandatory Issues: Service Mapping and Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC identifies mandatory issues that must be addressed. Service mapping describes how different Ethernet attachment circuit types (physical ports, single VLANs, or VLAN bundles) can be associated with a single service instance, even asymmetrically across sites. The frame format and VLAN tagging must follow 802.1ad conventions.

CE bridge protocol handling is critical because bridges run protocols like Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol (RSTP) or Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (MSTP) to manage loops and detect topology changes. The VPLS PE must either operate transparently with respect to these protocols (when the attachment circuit is port-based) or participate by peering with the customer's protocol (when the attachment circuit is VLAN-based). The 802.1ad bridge module provides the necessary reserved MAC addresses and protocol support to make this work.
sections.eli5: Bridges at the customer site run protocols to avoid loops. The provider must either stay out of the way or play along correctly. The PE model lets it do either, depending on what the customer plugs in.

sections.title: Mandatory Issues: Mesh, Multicast, and Topology
sections.content:
VPLS depends on a full mesh of pseudowires. If a pseudowire fails, the mesh becomes partial, which causes problems for bridges: broadcast storms, multiple frame copies, and potential loop formation in spanning tree. The RFC recommends using IEEE 802.1ag connectivity fault management procedures to detect partial mesh failures and notify the affected PEs quickly, preventing these issues.

Multicast and broadcast traffic in VPLS rely on ingress replication: the PE that receives a multicast packet replicates it to each other PE. When customer edge devices are bridges, multicast is especially important because bridge protocols use multicast for control messages. Using IGMP snooping can reduce unnecessary replication, but the RFC warns against using provider multicast distribution trees for customer traffic because they can cause control traffic and data to take different paths, leading to loop formation or disconnection in customer spanning trees.
sections.eli5: If a wire breaks, bridges see only part of the network and can create loops. The provider must notice breaks quickly. Also, broadcast messages from the customer's bridge protocol must take the same path as regular traffic, or the bridge thinks the network is broken and changes what it is doing.

sections.title: Optional Issues: Redundancy, Topology, and Learning
sections.content:
When customer sites are dual-homed to multiple PEs for redundancy, only one PE is active at a time. However, in the current design, the active PE replicates broadcast and multicast frames over all its pseudowires, even those that are blocked by redundancy mechanisms, wasting provider network bandwidth. The RFC recommends that PEs exchange information about which pseudowires are active so they can replicate only over active paths. Additionally, the PE's failure detection must be faster than the customer's spanning tree convergence time to prevent unnecessary topology changes in the customer network.

When customer networks have topology changes (due to link failures or loops being detected), they send topology change notification (TCN) messages. The PE must flush customer MAC addresses it has learned when a TCN arrives, so frames do not black-hole. Finally, when a PE is on the path for only one service instance (one ingress and one egress port), MAC address learning can be disabled because the path through that PE is fixed and all frames are simply forwarded in one direction.
sections.eli5: When the company has backup switches, the provider should notice which ones are active and not send duplicate traffic to the blocked ones. Also, when the company's network changes shape, the provider must forget old addresses so traffic does not disappear.
